tag: A militia educational cartoon from the North Carolina Piedmont
model: Bluey for family-length; Liberty's Kids for founding witnesses. Original show. Not those licenses.

cast.name: Bell
cast.role: Hopewell meeting-house bell. Rings the story. Not the Philadelphia Liberty Bell.

cast.name: Vee
cast.role: A girl named for Violet Wilson, whose marriages knit the command family.

cast.name: Lee
cast.role: A boy named for General William Lee Davidson. Coat too big on purpose.

episodes.title: The Bell of Hopewell
episodes.learn: This Bell lives at a meeting house on the Catawba. Philadelphia has a famous cracked bell too. Ours rings Piedmont stories.

panels.text: I hang in the pines of Mecklenburg. When I ring, the families come: Wilson, Davidson, Polk, Brevard, Alexander, Reese, Knox, Caldwell, Graham. They married each other so often the militia was almost one household.
Are you the Liberty Bell from Philadelphia?
No, child. That bell rang for a whole country. I ring for a river and a nest of hornets. Same liberty. Smaller steeple.
Then tell us the presidents who grew from this nest — Washington, Madison, Jackson, Polk, Lincoln.
I will. But first the families, or the presidents will sound like they fell from the sky. They did not.

episodes.title: Samuel Wilson’s Daughters
episodes.learn: Mary Wilson married Ezekiel Polk — grandfather line of President James Knox Polk. Violet Wilson married Major John Davidson of Rural Hill.

panels.text: Samuel Wilson farmed on this river. His daughters’ marriages are the map of the command family.
Mary married Ezekiel Polk. Their line runs to a boy named James Knox Polk — Knox for his other grandfather, who carried a captain’s name.
Violet married Major John Davidson. He signed Mecklenburg’s paper and kept Rural Hill. Their girl Isabella married Joseph Graham, the militia major who would not stay down.
Samuel’s son married Hannah Knox — daughter of Captain Patrick Knox, killed at Ramsour’s Mill. So Knox is not a stranger in this cartoon. He is in the house.
And Sarah Davidson married Alexander Caldwell, son of Dr. David Caldwell, who kept a school. Teachers in the blood, even when we are only enrolled.

episodes.title: The Hornet Nest
episodes.learn: Cornwallis called Mecklenburg a hornet nest. The families stung and scattered and came back.

panels.text: Why do people call us hornets?
Because a British general found Charlotte was not a place you sit down in. The militia of this family — Polk, Davidson, Graham, Alexander — kept stinging and flying.
Lt. Col. Thomas Polk called neighbors to the courthouse. Dr. Ephraim Brevard wrote. David Reese signed. The paper said the king’s law was vacant here.
A nest is a family. That is the joke and the truth.

episodes.title: The Horse Comes Home
episodes.learn: General William Lee Davidson, uncle to Major John and to Adlai Osborne — one family — fell at Cowan’s Ford, 1 February 1781. The horse from Rural Hill came home without him. We do not draw the shot.

panels.text: William Lee Davidson was a militia general. He had been at Germantown and Valley Forge. He married a Brevard. His father’s will named John Brevard and Alexander Osborne as guardians of the children — Adlai Osborne’s house.
He was uncle to Major John of Rural Hill, and uncle in the house of Adlai Osborne. One Davidson family, not two. The horse he rode that morning was from his nephew’s barn.
Major John lent him a horse from Rural Hill to ride to the Catawba, to stop Cornwallis at Cowan’s Ford.
The general fell in the river fog. The horse came home. That is how Major John knew. We ring once, and we do not make a game of it.
His baby son, also William Lee, was not yet a month old. That boy later married Betsy Lee Davidson, Major John’s daughter. Kin by marriage after the river.

episodes.title: Graham in the Pines
episodes.learn: Joseph Graham, militia, was shot near Charlotte in 1780 and left. Aunt Susie Alexander found him. He lived, married Isabella Davidson, and their son William A. Graham served North Carolina.

panels.text: Father and son: Joseph Graham in the war; William Alexander Graham in the peace — governor, senator. The cartoon is the father’s night in the pines.
Tarleton’s men dropped him. Aunt Susie Alexander, hunting cows, found him and got him home.
He married Isabella, Major John’s daughter. So Graham is not a guest. He is Wilson and Davidson too.
When a family finds you in the pines, that is militia. Not a costume. A cousin with a lantern.

episodes.title: Ephraim and Adlai
episodes.learn: One Davidson family: General William Lee is uncle to Major John and Adlai Osborne. Dr. Ephraim Brevard and Adlai, cousins, finished Princeton in 1768 under Witherspoon. Ephraim wrote Mecklenburg’s resolves and married a Polk.

panels.text: John Brevard’s boy Ephraim and Alexander Osborne’s boy Adlai walked to the same grammar, then to Nassau Hall, year 1768.
That is Witherspoon’s Princeton — the college our big hall wants to compete with. They learned moral philosophy, then came home.
Ephraim became the doctor who wrote. He married Col. Thomas Polk’s daughter. Adlai became the lawyer of Rowan, clerk of the court, a man of the committee.

General Davidson is uncle to Major John and to Adlai Osborne. One family. Ephraim and Adlai, cousins, walked to Princeton together. The guardians in the old will — John Brevard and Alexander Osborne — are that same house.

episodes.title: Washington Goes Home
episodes.learn: Washington commanded the army, then went home. Energy in the office, not a king in the man.

panels.text: Did our militia belong to Washington?
They belonged to the law and to North Carolina, and they answered when the Continental line needed a crossing held. Washington was the commander who would not keep the sword.
A king stays. A president goes home. That is the first lesson of presidents in this show.
Ring it once. We will need it when later men forget.

episodes.title: Madison’s Notebook
episodes.learn: Madison learned under Witherspoon too. The Constitution is a form to keep the Declaration’s end. He wrote notes so we could see the argument.

panels.text: Madison went to the same Princeton as Ephraim and Adlai, a few years later.
He kept a notebook at the Convention like a boy who knows he will have to explain it. Publius and Brutus both get a hearing in our big hall. Here we say: he wrote so the people could read.
Is the Constitution the bell or the steeple?
The Declaration is why I ring. The Constitution is the yoke I hang from. Without a yoke, a bell falls. Without a reason, a yoke is only iron.

episodes.title: Jackson and the People
episodes.learn: Jackson was a Carolina boy who said the people are the sovereign. Bank, Union, a hard hand. We teach the office, not a saint.

panels.text: Jackson is loud.
He is. He came from this same backcountry idea: the people, not a caucus of clerks. He broke a bank and held a Union and used a hard hand. This show will not make him a stuffed angel.
Our civics hall already keeps Jacksonian lessons. Here we only say: a president is still under the law, even a popular one.
Lex rex, children. The law is king. Even when the people cheer.

episodes.title: Cousin Polk
episodes.learn: James Knox Polk, eleventh president, comes down from Mary Wilson and Ezekiel Polk. Knox is the middle name on purpose.

panels.text: The boy from Mary Wilson’s line sat in the White House.
James Knox Polk. Mecklenburg blood, Tennessee house, a Knox in the name for the captain’s people. Lt. Col. Polk’s kin. This is why we taught the daughters first.
So a president can be a cousin from Rural Hill’s web.
A republic is supposed to work like that. Not a palace. A family that learned to read and to muster.

episodes.title: Lincoln’s Books
episodes.learn: Lincoln had no college. He copied Euclid, Shakespeare, the Bible, Blackstone. Slow to scratch, slow to forget. We do not make a war of this episode.

panels.text: Lincoln is not from Mecklenburg.
No. He is in this show because he learned like our meeting house: few books, copied, recited. That is the method of the bigger school on this git.
He said the Lyceum must be law, not the mob. Our general died at a ford under law, not under a riot.
Copy one proposition. Recite one speech. Then you have watched this episode for real. Films do not pass a Lincoln class. Neither do cartoons, unless you copy.
